---
title: "Correlated traits and assembly in trait space"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4,
                      eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE))
```

Species differ in several traits at once, and those traits rarely evolve independently.
This article shows how comdynamite simulates several correlated traits along a tree, how
selective regimes can change the rates, the correlations and the optima, and how community
assembly then uses distances in a space of several traits.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)
set.seed(4)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(60)
```

## Evolutionary rate matrices

Under multivariate Brownian motion, the changes of the traits per unit time have a covariance
matrix, the evolutionary rate matrix: its diagonal holds the rate of each trait and its
off-diagonal elements the evolutionary covariances. `rate_matrix()` builds it with the
structures that mvMORPH fits (Clavel et al. 2015). With one matrix for the whole tree:

```{r}
rate_matrix(c(1, 0.5), correlation = 0.8)
rate_matrix(1, correlation = 0.3, constraint = "equal", n_traits = 3)
```

With selective regimes, each regime can have its own matrix, constrained in the ways of
`mvMORPH::mvBM()`: proportional matrices, shared eigenvectors, the same variances or the same
correlations. Each matrix is drawn as the ellipse of the changes of two traits in one unit of
time.

```{r}
prop <- rate_matrix(c(1, 2), correlation = 0.6, constraint = "proportional",
                    scale = c(forest = 1, open = 3))
plot(prop) + ggplot2::ggtitle("proportional")
flip <- rate_matrix(c(1, 1), correlation = list(forest = 0.8, open = -0.8),
                    constraint = "variance")
plot(flip) + ggplot2::ggtitle("equal variances")
```

## Traits on a history of habitats

`trait_mk()` simulates a discrete character on the tree, here the habitat of each lineage,
with changes inside branches. `trait_ou()` takes that mapped history as `regimes`, so that
the rates (and, with `alpha > 0`, the optima) change at the moment the habitat changes.
`plot_traits()` draws the result as a phylomorphospace, with the branches coloured by habitat,
or, for one trait, as a traitgram.

```{r}
habitat <- trait_mk(tree, q = 0.4, states = c("forest", "open"))
x <- trait_ou(habitat, sigma2 = flip, regimes = habitat)
plot_traits(x, habitat, regimes = habitat)
plot_traits(x, habitat, traits = 1, regimes = habitat)
```

Optima can also differ between traits. With a matrix `theta`, one row per regime and one
column per trait, the open habitat below moves the optimum of the first trait only.

```{r}
theta <- rbind(forest = c(0, 0), open = c(4, 0))
y <- trait_ou(habitat, alpha = 2, sigma2 = rate_matrix(c(1, 1), correlation = 0.5),
               theta = theta, regimes = habitat)
plot_traits(y, habitat, regimes = habitat)
```

## Assembly in a space of several traits

`assemble_community()` removes species by their distances in trait space. With correlated
traits, Euclidean distances count the shared direction of variation more than once; the
Mahalanobis distance treats each independent direction as one axis, and `"standardized"`
divides each trait by its standard deviation in the pool. The help of `assemble_community()`
discusses which to choose. `plot_assembly()` shows the result in the metric of the assembly:
for filtering, the boundary of the filter around the optimum.

```{r}
z <- trait_ou(tree, sigma2 = rate_matrix(c(1, 4), correlation = 0.9))
plot_assembly(assemble_community(z, 20, rule = "filtering", optimum = c(0, 0))) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Euclidean")
plot_assembly(assemble_community(z, 20, rule = "filtering", optimum = c(0, 0),
                                 distance = "mahalanobis")) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Mahalanobis")
```

Under limiting similarity, the contours have half the smallest distance between the species
kept, so that they touch but do not overlap.

```{r}
plot_assembly(assemble_community(z, 20)) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Euclidean")
plot_assembly(assemble_community(z, 20, distance = "mahalanobis")) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Mahalanobis")
```

## A niche with several environmental axes

In the dynamic model, `simulate_metacommunity()` takes one set of traits per environmental
axis and a matrix `env` with one column per axis; the growth rate of a species is the product
of its responses to each axis. `as_mc_data()` keeps every axis, and `summary_stats()` uses the
first unless given another.

```{r}
land <- landscape_grid(side = 6)
temperature <- species_traits(tree)
moisture <- species_traits(tree, rmax_range = c(1, 1))
env <- cbind(temperature = land$env, moisture = rev(land$env))
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(land, list(temperature = temperature, moisture = moisture),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "phylo"), n_steps = 200, env = env)
sim
head(as_mc_data(sim)$traits)
```

## Validation

[`data-raw/validation_mvtraits.R`](https://github.com/diogoprov/comdynamite/blob/main/data-raw/validation_mvtraits.R)
compares `trait_ou()` with mvMORPH (version 1.2.3). Over 20000 simulations with two regimes
that change within branches, the covariances of the tips stayed within 2.9 Monte Carlo
standard errors of their expected value, \(\sum_k R_k \otimes C_k\) (mvMORPH's `mvSIM()`:
2.8), and under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process within 3.1 standard errors of the covariance of
Hansen (1997). Fitting `mvBM()` with the same constraint to simulated traits of 100 tips
recovered each structure, with the median of 30 fits within 9% of each element of the true
matrices.

## References

Clavel, J., Escarguel, G., & Merceron, G. (2015). mvMORPH: an R package for fitting
multivariate evolutionary models to morphometric data. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 6,
1311--1319. <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12420>

Hansen, T. F. (1997). Stabilizing selection and the comparative analysis of adaptation.
*Evolution*, 51, 1341--1351. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1558-5646.1997.tb01457.x>
